chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Khalid and Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, all from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya Al-Halbi, from Abu Khalid, from Marwak the pearl seller, from the one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He mentioned 'al-Raghbah' (desire/yearning) and displayed the inner side of his two palms towards the sky; and he said: 'Thus is 'al-Rahbah' (awe/reverence)', and he made the back of his palms towards the sky; and he said: 'Thus is 'at-Tadarru' (humble beseeching)', and he moved his fingers to the right and to the left; and he said: 'Thus is 'at-Tabattul' (devotion/earnestness)', and he raised his fingers once and lowered them once; and he said: 'Thus is 'al-Ibtihal' (supplication/calling out)', and he extended his hand facing his face towards the Qiblah; and he said: 'And there is no 'Ibtihal' until the tear flows'.

key_terms.الرَّغْبَة: Desire or yearning for God's bounty
key_terms.الرَّهْبَة: Awe or reverence for God's majesty
key_terms.الِابْتِهَال: Earnest invocation or calling out to God

ai.seo_question: What are the specific physical gestures and postures for different types of suppulation (dua) in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the nuanced somatic expressions of the heart during supplication, distinguishing between states of longing, fear, and humility through specific hand gestures. It emphasizes that authentic Ibtihal (earnest invocation) is intrinsically linked to emotional sincerity, marked by the flowing of tears, a concept deeply valued in Shia spiritual practice as the seal of the supplicant's presence before God.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad BinYahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Muhammad Bin Khalid and Al Husayn Bin Saeed, altogether from Al Nazar Bin Suweyd, from Yahya Al Halby, from Abu Khalid, from Marwak Baya’a Al Lulu, from the one who mentioned it, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup>, said,

‘The desire (الرَّغْبَةَ) was mentioned and he<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> displayed the front of the two palms towards the sky; (and said): ‘The awe (الرَّهْبَةُ) is like this’, and he<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> make the back of his<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> palm to be towards the sky; (and said): ‘And the beseeching (التَّضَرُّعُ) is like this’, and he<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> moved his<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> index finger to the right and the left; (and said): ‘The devotion (التَّبَتُّلُ) is like this’, and he<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> raised his<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> finger once and dropped it once; (and said): ‘The invocation (الِابْتِهَالُ) is like this’, and he<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> extended his<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> hand and turned his<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> face towards the Qiblah, (and said): ‘And there is no invocation until the tears flow’.
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Isa from Muhammad ibn Khalid and al-Husayn ibn Sa’Id all from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Yahya al-Halabi from abu Khalid from Marwan Bayya’al-Lu’lu from those whom he has mentioned (in his book) who has said the following:

“Once al-Raghbah (fondness) was mentioned before abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) and he raised his hands to the sky with his palms upward. He then turned the back of his hands upward to the sky and said, “This way is al-Rahbah (expressing anxiety). He moved his fingers right and left and said that such is al-Tadarru’ . He then raised his fingers and then lower them saying that such is al-Tabattul. He then stretched his hands in front of his face toward the Ka’bah saying that such is al-‘Ibtihal only when tears flow.’”
